description: A character essay on Jack O’Neill, how Richard Dean Anderson’s humor works with military leadership, grief, ensemble trust and the command decisions that shape Stargate SG-1.

historical_claims.anchor: The scene comes from *Window of Opportunity*, the fourth-season episode in which Jack and Teal'c are trapped in a repeating interval of time.
In the first-season episode *Cold Lazarus*, an alien crystal creates a duplicate of him.
In later interviews about the series' origins, co-creator Jonathan Glassner recalled Anderson's insistence that his Jack could not remain as relentlessly grim as the film character.

historical_claims.anchor: In *Abyss*, from season six, Jack is captured by Ba'al, who subjects him to repeated torture and death, then uses a sarcophagus to restore him and begin again.
*A Hundred Days*, in which a catastrophe leaves Jack stranded on Edora for months while his team struggles to reach him.
An archaeologist named Malikai wants to use an Ancient device to return to a period before the death of his wife.
Jack knows exactly what is wrong with that hope, but not because his experience has given him superior scientific knowledge.
In *A Matter of Time*, the Stargate locks onto a world threatened by a black hole.
*Shades of Grey* takes the problem of authority from another angle.
Jack deliberately accepts another download of that knowledge, understanding from experience that it may kill him.
The sequence ends with Ancient defenses saving Earth, and with Jack preserved in stasis pending rescue.
By the beginning of season eight, Jack has been rescued and promoted to brigadier general, taking command of Stargate Command.
Samantha Carter becomes a lieutenant colonel.
Consider *Zero Hour*, in which the newly promoted general confronts an apparently endless succession of problems at the SGC.
